questions.q: Why does momentum_signal convert returns to log returns before taking a rolling sum?
options: Log returns are required by pandas for any rolling operation
It replaces a rolling product (which would need .rolling().apply(), calling Python once per window) with a rolling sum that stays fully vectorized
Log returns are always larger in magnitude, which improves accuracy
It is purely a style preference with no performance effect
questions.explain: log1p/expm1 turns compounding (a product) into addition (a sum), so .rolling().sum() can compute it without ever calling a Python function per window.

questions.q: Why is the rolling z-score the one function wrapped in @njit instead of staying in plain pandas?
options: Numba is required for all numerical code
It has no clean vectorized pandas form — it needs a trailing mean and standard deviation recomputed at every point — and it was identified as the hot path
Pandas cannot compute a mean or standard deviation at all
@njit is applied to every function in the package as a default
questions.explain: The lesson reserves Numba for the one calculation without a clean vectorized equivalent, consistent with the kickoff's plan to hand-optimize only the actual hot path.

questions.q: In backtest_returns, what does weights.shift(lag) accomplish?
options: It randomizes the weights to simulate noise
It applies a prior day's weights to the current day's return, preventing the backtest from trading on information not yet available (lookahead bias)
It removes rows with missing data
It converts weights from long-only to long-short
questions.explain: Shifting the weights forward by `lag` days means today's return is multiplied by a weight decided on an earlier day, avoiding lookahead bias.

questions.q: Why does the test suite use np.testing.assert_allclose instead of a plain == comparison?
options: assert_allclose is faster to type
The log-sum-exp computation and the manually compounded value are mathematically equal but can differ slightly due to floating-point rounding order
== does not work on pandas Series under any circumstances
assert_allclose ignores incorrect results
questions.explain: Two mathematically equivalent floating-point computations can differ in the last few bits because of rounding order, so allclose-style comparisons with a tolerance are the correct test.

questions.q: What problem does driving the pipeline from a Hydra config.yaml (lookback, quantiles, lag, seed) solve?
options: It makes the code run faster
It lets two runs with the same config produce the same logged results, which is what reproducibility means in practice
It eliminates the need for any tests
It replaces the need for a data layer entirely
questions.explain: Centralizing every run parameter in one config file, combined with a seeded generator and logging, is what makes a run's results explainable and repeatable later.
